passage: Ramesh, my boy, put your head here on my knee, the oil is warm. I am Yamini, your Dadi. When I was small, we had a mango tree behind the house, and my sister and I would race to be first under it when the wind blew. Once I got there and found a green snake curled up asleep under the fruit! You are giggling. Yes, I screamed too. Now tell me, why did I not run away? You say because I was frozen. Very good guess. You ask me such good questions, beta. I will tell you the rest of the mango story tomorrow, and you must remember where I stopped.

qa.q: What did Dadi's sister and she race to do when the wind blew?
qa.a: They raced to be first under the mango tree.

qa.q: What might Ramesh be feeling as he rests his head on his grandmother's knee?
qa.a: He probably feels warm, safe and curious, since he giggles, guesses answers and asks good questions. 🙂

qa.q: What could Ramesh do to keep these moments meaningful?
qa.a: He can keep listening, ask about the parts he wants to know and remember where the story stopped so it can be picked up tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel when Ramesh asks her questions?
qa.a: Dadi likely feels happy and valued, since she praises his questions and promises to tell the rest tomorrow.

grounding: A grandmother tells old stories while oiling her grandchild's hair; he listens, asks questions and feels warmth and belonging.

passage:
'Sit still, Noor, or the oil will go in your eyes.' Nani's fingers pressed warm coconut oil into her scalp.
'Tell the one about the flood, Nani. When you were small.'
'Again? You've heard it fifty times.'
'Fifty-one, then.'
Nani laughed. 'The river came right up to our steps. My father put us children on the roof with the goat.'
'The goat's name was Badal,' Noor said.
'You remember everything.'
'Why didn't you go to the school building?'
'Good question. It was on lower ground. Your great-grandfather was wiser than he looked.'
Tanvir poked his head round the door. 'Is it the goat story? I want the goat story!'
'Sit, then. You're next.'
'I don't have long hair!'
'Then you get the oil only.' Noor giggled and leaned back against Nani's knees.

qa.q: How does Noor feel during the hair-oiling stories?
qa.a: Warm, loved and content; she asks for the story again and leans back against Nani's knees 🤍

qa.q: What does Noor do that makes the stories matter?
qa.a: She listens, remembers details like the goat's name, and asks questions such as why they didn't go to the school building.

qa.q: How does Nani feel when Noor remembers everything?
qa.a: Pleased and touched; she laughs and praises Noor's memory.

grounding: A girl loves her grandmother's stories while her hair is oiled, listening, asking questions and remembering.

passage: Every winter Sunday in Kolkata, Thakuma oiled my hair on the terrace, and my cousin Indu and I took turns sitting on the low stool in front of her. I'm Bidisha, and those mornings are the warmest thing I remember. The mustard oil smelled sharp, the sun was soft, and Thakuma told stories: how she walked to school with a lantern in Barisal, how she once hid a stray kitten in her rice tin. I always asked questions. 'What colour was the kitten? Did your mother find out?' Indu said I asked too many. Thakuma said questions keep stories alive. Now I write them in a green notebook, so I won't forget. Even today, whenever my hair is oiled, I can hear her voice.

qa.q: Where did Thakuma hide a stray kitten?
How does Bidisha feel remembering those Sunday mornings?
qa.a: Warm and loved; Bidisha calls them the warmest thing remembered and can still hear Thakuma's voice.

qa.q: What does Bidisha do to keep the stories?
qa.a: Asked questions while listening, and now writes the stories in a green notebook.

qa.q: How does Thakuma see Bidisha's questions?
qa.a: As a good thing; she says questions keep stories alive.

grounding: A child looks back on a grandmother's stories told while oiling hair, and keeps them by asking and writing them down.
